cards.title: Who decides the way?
cards.body:
A message from your home to a [[server]] in another country can pass through a dozen or more machines, and it gets there in a fraction of a second.

No single machine plans that whole journey. Instead, each machine along the way makes one small decision: *where should this [[packet]] go next?*

cards.title: Routers and routing tables
cards.body:
A **router** is a device that connects different [[networks|network]] and passes [[packets|packet]] between them. When a packet arrives, the router reads its destination address and checks its **routing table**: a list that says, for each group of addresses, which neighbour to send packets to next.

A router doesn't know the whole route, only the next step. It's like following signposts at road junctions: each one just points you the right way from *there*. Each step along the way (from your device to the first router, then from router to router) is called a **hop**.

cards.title: Switches, and the box at home
cards.body:
Inside one [[network]], devices are usually joined by a **switch**, which passes data between devices on that same network.

Your home router is really three boxes in one: a **router** (the way out to the internet), a **switch** (joining your home devices) and a **Wi-Fi access point** (the part that sends out the Wi-Fi signal).

cards.prompt: Get the [[packet]] from the **laptop** to the **web [[server]]**. There's more than one way.
cards.explanation: Both routes work. The internet is built with lots of connections between [[routers|router]], so there's usually more than one way to reach a destination. Each router uses its [[routing table]] to pick the next [[hop]], often the one that's shortest or least busy. Having spare routes also means the internet keeps working when one connection fails.
cards.hint: Start at the laptop and follow the links from node to node until you reach the server. Any route along the links will do.
cards.nudge: Each step has to follow a line that joins two nodes. Start at the laptop and only move along the links you can see.

cards.prompt:
A [[packet]] travels:

laptop → home router → [[ISP]] router → main internet router → the [[server]]'s router → web server

How many **routers** does it pass through?
cards.explanation: The routers are the home router, the ISP router, the main internet router and the server's router: **4**. The laptop and the web server are the two ends of the journey, where the packet starts and finishes, so they aren't routers.
cards.hint: Go along the journey and count only the routers. Where the packet starts and finishes aren't routers.
cards.nudge: The laptop and the web server are the two ends of the journey, not routers. Count only the boxes in between.

cards.prompt: Match each device to its job.

pairs.right: Provides a service, like a website
A device a person uses to send and receive

cards.explanation: A **router** links different networks and picks the next [[hop]]. A **switch** connects devices inside one network. A **server** provides something, like web pages, to other devices. A **laptop** is an end device: packets start or finish there.
cards.hint: One device links different networks, one joins devices inside one network, one provides a service, and one is used by a person.
cards.nudge: A router works between networks, while a switch works inside one network. Try sorting those two out first.

cards.title: Seeing the hops with traceroute
cards.body:
You can see the [[routers|router]] your [[packets|packet]] pass through using a tool called **traceroute** (on Windows it's called `tracert`).

The first line just repeats where you're going. After that it prints one numbered line per [[hop]], in order: hop 1, hop 2, and so on. Each line shows the router's address and three times, because traceroute tests each hop three times. The times are in **ms** ([[milliseconds|millisecond]], thousandths of a second), and they show how long the router took to reply.

The last line is the destination itself.

Some routers are set up not to answer traceroute. Their line shows `* * *` instead of times, but they still pass your packets on.

cards.prompt: Run `traceroute example.com` on this [[Linux]] laptop, then find the address of the **first [[hop]]**.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: List each router between you and example.com

success.question: What is the address of the first hop?

cards.explanation: Hop 1 is `192.168.1.1`, a [[private address]]: it's your **home router**, the [[default gateway]] you saw with `ipconfig`. Every trip out of your home starts there. Hops 2 to 4 are routers belonging to internet companies, and hop 5 is example.com itself. Notice the times grow as [[packets|packet]] travel further.
cards.hint: Run `traceroute example.com`, then find the line numbered 1. The very first line of output only repeats where you're going.
cards.nudge: Hop 1 is the line that starts with the number 1, not the top line. Type that hop's address exactly, without the times.

cards.prompt:
In a traceroute, hop 3 looks like this:

```
 3  * * *
```

But hops 4 and 5 still show up after it. What does `* * *` most likely mean?

options.text: That router didn't answer traceroute, but it still passed the packets on

options.nudge: If the router at hop 3 were broken, could packets still reach hops 4 and 5? Look at what comes after it.

options.text: All the packets were lost forever at hop 3
options.nudge: Hops 4 and 5 still answered, so packets must have got past hop 3.
Traceroute gives one line per hop, so something is there at hop 3. It just didn't send back an answer.

cards.explanation: Each `*` means *no reply arrived in time*. Many routers are set up to ignore traceroute's test messages, or to answer them last when they're busy. Hops 4 and 5 answered, so packets clearly **did** get through hop 3: the router is there and working, it just stayed quiet.
cards.hint: Look at what happens after hop 3. If hops 4 and 5 still reply, what does that tell you about the packets?

cards.prompt: **Router 2 is down** (it has stopped working). Find a route from the **laptop** to the **web [[server]]** that avoids it.
cards.explanation: Every working route goes through **Router 4**, the only other router linked to the server. You can reach it through Router 1 or Router 3, and both count. Router 1 still works, it's only its link onwards to Router 2 that leads nowhere. This is what routers do automatically when something fails: they [[update]] their [[routing tables|routing-table]] and send [[packets|packet]] around the problem.
cards.hint: [[Router]] 2 is broken, so no route can go through it. Find another router that links to the web server, then work back to the laptop.
cards.nudge: Any route through Router 2 fails. Check which other router has a link to the web server, and find a way to reach it.

cards.prompt:
Every packet carries a **time to live (TTL)**: a [[hop]] limit. Each router lowers it by 1. If a router brings it down to 0, it throws the packet away and sends back a message saying so, which reveals the router's address.

[[Traceroute]] uses this trick. Put its steps in order.

items.label: Send a packet with a TTL of 1
The first router lowers the TTL to 0, drops the packet and replies
Send a packet with a TTL of 2
The second router lowers the TTL to 0, drops the packet and replies
Keep adding 1 to the TTL until the destination itself replies

cards.explanation: A TTL of 1 runs out at the **first** router, so it replies and traceroute learns hop 1. A TTL of 2 gets one router further before running out, revealing hop 2, and so on. Traceroute keeps going until the destination answers. The TTL exists so that a lost packet can't loop around the internet forever.
cards.hint: A TTL of 1 runs out at the first router. Think about what a bigger TTL would reach, and when traceroute can stop.
cards.nudge: Each packet's TTL decides how far it gets before a router drops it and replies. Each send comes before the reply it causes.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **router** passes [[packets|packet]] between [[networks|network]]. It checks its **routing table** to choose the next step, not the whole route.
- Each step from router to router is a **hop**. There's usually more than one possible route.
- A **switch** connects devices within one network.
- **Traceroute** (`tracert` on Windows) lists each hop. The first hop is usually your home router, and `* * *` means a router didn't reply.

Next: what happens when packets take different roads.
